tagline: Know what every asset is — so someone can own it.
lore: Carl Linnaeus, the father of taxonomy, gave every living thing its name and rank — here he names every asset by what it is: server, desktop, camera, printer, switch, PLC, cloud instance.
problem: You can't own, scope or prioritize an asset you can't name. In most estates a large share of assets carry no class at all, so they fall out of ownership, scan policy and reporting — and nobody can say whether they are servers, printers or PLCs.
does: Linnaeus classifies every asset from the tags the pack has written, and shows exactly what is still unclassified. From operating-system fingerprints and device signals he suggests classes for the untagged assets, groups them into cohorts you can approve, and writes the tags.

glance.caption: Linnaeus's At a glance on a 128-asset lab: only 6 assets classified (4.7%) and 122 unclassified — 40 of them with an OS or device signal ready to tag; 34 on an unsupported OS; 29 unclassified assets with an open critical, and the riskiest one named.

capabilities: the pack's own taxonomy — Asset Inventory, IoT, Device Type, OS — rolled up into Windows, Linux, macOS, Server, Workstation, Mobile, IoT, OT, network, hypervisor, cloud and Unclassified.

Server, Desktop, Laptop, Workstation, Phone / Tablet, Camera, Printer, NAS, VoIP, UPS / Power, Badge Reader, Switch, Router, Firewall, Wireless Access Point, Load Balancer, Hypervisor, PLC, HMI, RTU — offered as you tag, and each maps to its class.
untagged assets grouped by Nessus's own device type (printer, camera, switch, firewall …) or by detected OS ("Windows Server 2022 — 40 assets"), each cohort one approval away from a tag.
OS families and versions for the untagged assets, with a confidence rating for each fingerprint.
Tag by OS in plain English
"tag all my assets by OS with a confidence over 70" becomes a plan you review before anything is written.
a zoomable sunburst of class → subnet → software and Docker, down to each asset (which opens in Argos).
KEV and critical findings, cloud assets, and classified assets with no owner — so the unclassified bucket becomes a ranked worklist.
how: Linnaeus reads tags, OS fields, OS-identification and Nessus Device Type plugin output, and device signals from your local navi.db. An asset counts as cloud only when navi holds a real AWS, Azure or GCP id for it — navi stores a missing one as a blank, which is not cloud. Class lists page on the server. Tags use the scheme Asset Inventory : <facet>: <value> (Class, OS, Device Type, App), written behind the write gate and a confirm.
who: Asset and CMDB owners, vulnerability management teams scoping scans and policies, and anyone closing the gap between "discovered" and "owned".
better: Cerberus's IoT tags and Linnaeus's classes share one inventory scheme. Classified assets are what Terminus assigns owners to and Anubis calibrates; On the Scent's unclassified card opens Linnaeus on that list, and Covenant re-applies the class tags on its schedule.
cta: Let Linnaeus name your estate — you can't own what you can't classify.
